# Build a Simple Personal Budget Spreadsheet Using Any AI Assistant

**By the end of this guide, you'll have a working monthly budget in Excel, Google Sheets, or Apple Numbers — even if you've never built a spreadsheet before.** You'll simply ask an AI assistant (think of it as a chat-style helper that writes things for you) to design the structure, then copy the result into your favorite spreadsheet app. No formulas memorising, no finance jargon, no fuss.

## Before you start
- An account with any AI assistant. ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, and DeepSeek all work for this task — pick whichever you already have. Most have a free tier.
- A free spreadsheet app: Microsoft Excel (often pre-installed on Windows), Apple Numbers (on Mac), or Google Sheets (free in any browser at sheets.new).
- About 15 minutes the first time. A bit less once you've done it.

## Step 1 — Open your AI assistant
Visit the website of your chosen AI assistant in a browser tab, or open its app on your phone. Sign in if needed. You'll see a chat box — usually a large text field at the bottom of the screen with placeholder text like "Message ChatGPT" or "Ask Gemini" inside it. If you don't have an account yet, look for a "Sign up" or "Get started" button; sign-up usually takes under a minute with an email address. Once you're in, the chat sits quietly waiting — the AI won't reply until you send something in Step 2. If your assistant offers a model selector (a small drop-down at the top of the chat), the default option is fine for budget work; no need to change it.

You'll know it worked when you can see the empty chat box and your cursor is blinking inside it.

## Step 2 — Send the budget prompt
Click inside the chat box and type (or paste) your request. Press Enter, or tap the small upward-pointing paper-plane icon ➤ next to the box, to send. Within a few seconds, the AI starts typing a reply, and a budget table usually appears — complete with column headers like "Category", "Planned", "Actual", and a few sample rows. Some assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) also offer a downloadable spreadsheet file; look for a small spreadsheet icon or "Download" link above the reply. If you see a paperclip 📎 icon for attachments, ignore it; you don't need to upload anything.

💬 Example: "Design a simple monthly budget spreadsheet for a single person earning a regular salary. Include columns for Category (Rent, Groceries, Transport, Utilities, Entertainment, Savings, Other), Planned amount, Actual amount, and Difference. Add 2 example rows per category. Keep it under 20 rows total."

You'll know it worked when the AI replies with a clearly formatted table — or a downloadable file link.

## Step 3 — Check what the AI produced
Read the reply slowly. You'll usually see one of three things: (a) a neat table with rows and columns inside the chat, (b) a downloadable spreadsheet file, or (c) plain text describing the layout. Look for sensible categories (housing, food, transport, savings), clear column headers, and at least one mention of a formula — typically a "Difference" or "Total" column that subtracts one number from another. If the response feels too complex (mentions macros, pivot tables, or technical jargon), just reply asking for a simpler version. If the AI gave you plain text instead of a table, ask it to "format that as a table" in the same chat — it usually complies in one reply. Don't worry if the numbers are placeholders; you'll swap them for your own in Step 6.

You'll know it worked when you can clearly see columns, rows, and at least one total or formula reference in the reply.

## Step 4 — Open your spreadsheet app
Switch to (or open) your spreadsheet app: Excel on Windows, Numbers on Mac, or Google Sheets in any browser (sheets.new is the fastest way to start). You'll land on a blank grid — columns labeled A, B, C across the top, rows numbered 1, 2, 3 down the side. In Google Sheets, click the colorful "+" button to start a new blank spreadsheet. In Excel, choose "Blank workbook". If spreadsheets are new to you, know this: each little rectangle is called a "cell", and you click one to type into it. The cursor blinks in the top-left cell (A1), waiting for your first entry.

You'll know it worked when you see an empty grid of cells ready to receive your budget.

## Step 5 — Copy the AI's table into your spreadsheet
If the AI gave you a downloadable file, click "Download" and open it in Excel or Google Sheets — it lands as a ready-to-edit spreadsheet, and you can skip straight to Step 6. If the AI gave you a table inside the chat, click the small "Copy" icon that appears when you hover over the table (or highlight the text manually, then press Ctrl+C on Windows or Cmd+C on Mac). Click cell A1 in your empty spreadsheet and paste with Ctrl+V or Cmd+V. The categories and column headers appear neatly in row 1, with example data filling the rows below. If the paste comes out as one long paragraph instead of a grid, undo with Ctrl+Z and try Ctrl+Shift+V instead — most apps offer a "paste as plain text" option that cleans up the formatting.

You'll know it worked when the AI's budget rows are sitting in your spreadsheet, ready to edit.

## Step 6 — Add your real numbers and a totals row
Click each cell in the "Actual" or "Amount" column and type your own real spending for the past month — rough estimates are fine if you don't have receipts handy. Then click an empty cell directly below your last row and type a label like "Total". In the cell next to it (one column to the right), type =SUM(B2:B10), replacing B2 and B10 with the first and last row numbers of your actual data. Press Enter, and that cell instantly shows the sum. If your spreadsheet puts amounts in column C or D instead, change the letter to match. If you see #REF! or #VALUE! instead of a number, double-check the formula and the range — usually one cell was empty or the letters don't line up with your data.

You'll know it worked when the Total cell shows a single dollar figure that updates automatically as you change any of the amounts above it.

## Step 7 — Save the file and make it yours
Save your file: in Google Sheets, click the title at the top-left to rename it (it saves automatically); in Excel, press Ctrl+S. From here, you can add new categories by typing into new rows, duplicate the sheet for a new month (look for a small "+" at the bottom of the screen), or come back to the AI assistant for more formulas like =AVERAGE() to see your typical weekly grocery spend. Try one small change right now — edit a number and watch the Total update. That single moment is when spreadsheets start to feel less like a chore and more like a quiet little superpower.

You'll know it worked when you've saved a file with your name on it, full of your real numbers, and the totals update themselves whenever you change anything.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking for "the best budget spreadsheet".** There's no universal best, and the AI may invent complex features you don't need. Stick to simple columns (Category, Planned, Actual, Difference) and add complexity later only if you genuinely want it.
- **Pasting a screenshot of the AI's table into your spreadsheet app.** Most apps treat images as pictures, not data — so the cells stay empty. Use copy-and-paste from the text table, or download the file the AI offers.
- **Trusting the AI's placeholder numbers as personal advice.** The example figures are made up to show structure, not to recommend how you should spend. Replace them with your own real spending, and treat any rule-of-thumb percentages the AI mentions as a starting point rather than gospel.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** A 10-minute weekly glance at your "Actual" column tells you where your money actually goes — usually a few small surprises (daily coffees, ride-shares, app subscriptions) you can adjust without much pain.
- **For your business or work:** The same template scales to a side-project budget, a freelance invoice tracker, or a small team's monthly expenses — just rename the categories.
- **If you're just getting started:** Open one AI assistant, paste the prompt from Step 2, and download whatever it gives you. Don't try to perfect it. A rough budget you actually use beats a perfect one gathering dust in a folder.

## Try it now
Open your favorite AI assistant right now, paste the prompt from Step 2, and download the spreadsheet it produces. Spend two minutes renaming one column to something that matters to you — "Coffee", "Rent", "Dog walk" — and you're already further along than most people ever get.
